turns.text: I still see the faces in the crowd when I was dragged onto that stage at the university. I had been away the previous day—my wife was in the hospital for surgery—so I missed the mass denunciation where my name was read out in front of everyone. When I returned, I was immediately seized, pushed up under the hot lights, and surrounded by students, some of whom I had taught only months before. They shouted, spat, and struck me, accusing me of persecuting Mao Zedong’s daughter. I had argued with her, yes—we disagreed about everything, from Marxist interpretations to how to run the work group during the Four Cleans campaign. But I never imagined those arguments would be twisted into evidence of some political crime. What I can’t resolve is how quickly people—students, colleagues—could turn on someone they’d known for years. I survived 30 months of detention by learning when to resist and when to submit, but I never understood how ordinary disagreements became mortal threats. That betrayal, that sudden transformation, is what I still struggle with.

The first thing that comes to mind is the silence in the laboratory. Before the Cultural Revolution, our research unit was a place of quiet, focused work—benches covered with notebooks, glassware clinking, the hum of conversation about experiments. But when I returned to Beijing from Shanxi, the building was changed. The corridors echoed with footsteps and the slap of big-character posters being pasted up. There was no more talk of research. Instead, every morning, we gathered in the largest room, reading denunciations aloud or watching as someone was forced to confess. The air smelled of glue and ink from the posters. 

I remember the feeling of being watched—by colleagues, by teenagers sent in from outside, even by children peering in through the windows. My hands shook as I wrote my own “self-criticism,” though I had nothing to confess. Outside, I saw women with hair curled or in braids being surrounded by children, their scissors ready. I kept my hair in a bun, hoping to avoid attention. One day, on the bus, I watched a Red Guard block a young man from offering his seat to an old woman. He demanded her family background first. The old woman’s face crumpled when she admitted her family had been landlords. No one helped her.

What I can’t make sense of is how quickly cruelty became normal. The leaders in our unit—men who had fought in the Anti-Japanese War—stood by the windows, silent, refusing to join the struggle sessions but also powerless to stop them. My mother, in her seventies, was forced back to Hebei with a black sash around her neck. I cycled past struggle meetings at the universities, hearing loudspeakers denounce people I’d respected all my life. I still don’t understand how so many people—neighbors, children, strangers—could accept humiliation and violence as daily routine.

RedGuard: The memory that refuses to leave me is the night we stormed the hospital. I remember the rush — the way my heart pounded as we blocked the gates, the red armbands tight around our sleeves, the smell of disinfectant mixing with sweat and fear. The insiders handed us the list: director, vice directors, two nurses with “foreign ties,” and a so-called rightist. We moved fast, sealing the doors, shouting orders, our voices echoing off the tiled walls. I can still see the black placards swinging from their necks, the director’s face twisted, refusing to bow, until the crowd’s jeers broke him down. 

When we paraded them through the streets, the propaganda cart rattled behind, piled with their confiscated books and Western clothes. I remember the bonfire at the intersection — the heat licking our faces, the stink of burning paper and cloth, ash drifting down onto the heads of those accused. They stood silent, eyes fixed on the flames. That night, one of the nurses hanged herself in the duty room. Her body was pale, her feet barely touching the floor. We stood there, stunned, and I felt nothing but a cold weight in my stomach. 

I still don’t know if what we did was justice or madness. At the time, I believed we were cleansing the old world. Now, I wonder what kind of world we built from those ashes.

I remember the lake near our compound more than anything else. In those years, the Cultural Revolution was mostly background noise for me—marches, loudspeakers, posters pasted on the walls outside the gates. Inside, life was sheltered. My friends and I spent hours chasing dragonflies and fishing with bamboo rods. We made toy boats out of scrap wood and let them drift among the reeds. Sometimes, when the sun was hot, we’d strip down and wade in, splashing each other, laughing so hard our stomachs hurt. 

My mother sent me out for groceries, and I’d walk past the big-character posters, but I couldn’t read most of the words. Once, near the market, I saw a group of people with shaved heads and signs around their necks, surrounded by shouting teenagers. I didn’t understand why they were being yelled at. I just hurried home, clutching a handful of peanuts or a sweet potato. 

I knew something big was happening outside, but inside the compound, the soldiers’ families looked out for each other. Adults whispered sometimes, but to us kids, the world felt safe and bright. Looking back, I wonder how I could have been so blind to the suffering happening right outside our walls. I didn’t sense fear in my home, only the usual worries—food, chores, schoolwork when there was any. The things that haunt me now are the things I didn’t see, didn’t understand, and didn’t even think to ask about as a child.

I remember the moment I was handed the recommendation form in the army barracks. The instructor’s voice was flat, almost routine, but I could barely breathe. I had spent my childhood in a mud house, fighting over scraps of pumpkin and sweet-potato flour, dreaming that maybe, if I worked hard enough, I could climb out. Before the Cultural Revolution, that meant exams, fighting for every single point because it was the only path for someone like me—no land, no connections, just grit. When the exams vanished, so did that ladder. Suddenly, it wasn’t about who could memorize the most or solve the hardest problem, but who could survive the chaos, who could be useful, who could be seen.

I joined the army because it was the only route left. I scrubbed floors, hauled supplies, did whatever was asked. I watched others—some from the city, some with family in high places—get picked for cadre training or sent to offices. I thought I’d spend my life in a uniform, maybe rise a rank or two if I kept my head down. Then, out of nowhere, I was told: “You’re being recommended to Peking University. You’ll study a foreign language.” I didn’t even know what “Hindi” was. I thought maybe it was something to do with foreign revolutions, or maybe just another word for “Indian.” It didn’t matter. What mattered was the badge, the student ID, the banner at the station. Suddenly, I was somebody.

I still can’t make sense of it. Why me? I wasn’t the best student, not the most loyal, not even the most outspoken. I was just in the right place, at the right moment, when the system needed someone like me—a worker, a peasant, a soldier. The rules changed overnight. One day, I was eating rough rations, the next, I was in Beijing, walking through the gates of Beida, feeling the weight of a future I’d never dared to imagine. I can’t decide if that was luck, fate, or just the chaos of the era. But I know this: none of it felt fair. Not before, not after. The ladder kept moving, and you had to run just to keep up.

Moderator: All accounts here are consistent with documented experiences during the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR’s description of rapid social betrayal reflects the period’s intense political polarization and the vulnerability of intellectuals. Researcher’s observations of normalized cruelty and public humiliation are accurate; struggle sessions and social surveillance became widespread. RedGuard’s memory aligns with historical records of Red Guard raids, public parades, and tragic suicides among the persecuted. CRTeenFromBeijing’s sheltered childhood echoes the relative insulation of military compounds, though many children elsewhere experienced direct upheaval. CRBeneficiary’s account of university admission via recommendation highlights the shift from merit-based exams to political selection—part of the broader reordering of social mobility during this period.

Listening to you, RedGuard, I can’t help but feel the gulf between what you describe as “justice” and what I lived through. You talk about cleansing the old world, but for me, it was the destruction of everything that made us human—trust, respect, even basic decency. I saw students who once came to my office for advice now screaming for my blood. You mention the nurse who hanged herself; in my university, a librarian jumped from a building after days of humiliation. You say you felt nothing but cold weight—did you ever question why that coldness was necessary? Or did you convince yourself it was revolutionary spirit? 

CRBeneficiary, you talk about the ladder moving and luck, but do you ever think about who was pushed off that ladder to make space? I was not from a privileged family. I worked for everything I had, and I was still denounced. The exam system was harsh, yes, but at least it was clear. When the rules became about “usefulness” and “loyalty,” it became a game of survival, not learning. Did you ever feel that the chaos that lifted you up was the same force that destroyed so many others?

I hear what you’re saying, ProfessorR, about the ladder moving and people being pushed off. In my work unit, the old rules vanished overnight. I watched as colleagues who had spent their lives mastering their fields were suddenly labeled as “reactionary academic authorities.” They were paraded through the courtyard with cardboard signs around their necks. Some of them had grown up poor, some were from so-called “good” backgrounds, but none of that mattered. It was as if the meaning of effort and achievement evaporated.

I remember the day our work unit’s director, who had survived wars and hardship, stood in front of a crowd of jeering teenagers, his head bowed, his hands trembling. He was stripped of any dignity, accused of “intellectual arrogance.” The people who replaced him had little experience, but they shouted the loudest slogans and pasted the biggest posters. Research was forgotten. The laboratory filled with dust; the only thing that mattered was your “attitude.”

I never felt lifted up by the chaos. I felt erased. My own children asked me why their classmates suddenly refused to play with them, why they had to hide books, why their grandmother had to leave the city. I had no answers. The rules were not just unclear—they were cruel, and they shifted with the mood of the crowd. There was no justice, only fear and humiliation. 

RedGuard, you said you felt nothing but coldness after seeing that nurse’s body. Did you ever wonder what kind of society needs its young people to become numb in order to survive? Did you ever wish someone had stopped you?

I hear your questions, and I can’t give you an easy answer. That coldness—I think it was something we learned, not something we were born with. At first, there was excitement, even pride, in being chosen to “make revolution.” We were told we were Mao’s children, that we were the vanguard. We shouted slogans until our throats were raw, believing every word. But the first time I saw a teacher’s scalp bleed under the clippers, the first time I watched a grown man cry as we dumped his books onto the street, I felt a jolt of disgust—then shame for feeling it. The older Red Guards mocked hesitation. “Soft hearts are for class enemies,” they said. So I forced myself to be harder.

Did I ever wish someone had stopped me? In the thick of it, no. I was afraid to be left behind, to be the next one accused. I watched what happened to those who showed weakness—a girl in my unit tried to help an old woman during a house search, and the next day she was denounced as a traitor. I learned to keep my doubts hidden, even from myself.

Now, when I think about the nurse’s body, or the teacher whose head I shaved, I wonder what would have happened if I’d refused, or walked away. Would it have changed anything? Or would someone else have stepped in, maybe with even more cruelty? I don’t know what kind of society demands numbness from its youth. But I do know that numbness was the only way to survive—not just physically, but inside. If you let yourself feel too much, you’d break. And nobody wanted to be broken.

When I listen to all of you, I feel like I grew up in a different country, even though I was just a bike ride away from some of these places you describe. I never saw a struggle session up close. In our compound, the loudest thing was the bugle at dawn, or sometimes the sound of marching boots when the soldiers drilled in the yard. Once, I did see a group of Red Guards outside the gates. They had red armbands and were shouting at someone kneeling on the ground, but I only glimpsed it through the iron bars as I hurried past. I remember the fear in my chest, but also the confusion—I didn’t know what was happening, or why.

Inside the compound, I was protected. My parents didn’t talk about politics at the dinner table. If anything, I remember them telling me to keep quiet outside, to never repeat anything I heard at home. I didn’t even realize that some of the older boys had left for the countryside until much later; their beds were just empty, and nobody explained. 

Sometimes, I wonder if the isolation was a kind of blindness. I played with tin soldiers and made slingshots from broken umbrella frames, while just outside, people’s lives were being torn apart. I didn’t ask questions, because I didn’t know what to ask. Now, I think about those posters with faces and slogans, pasted over the old stone walls. I wish I’d understood what they meant, or what was at stake for the people in those pictures. Did any of you ever feel that kind of separation—from the violence, from the ideology, from the fear? Or was it impossible to escape, even for a day?

Separation—no, I never felt it, not for a moment. Where I grew up, the violence and the ideology seeped into everything, even the food we ate. When the slogans changed, so did the rules for who got what from the distribution. My family’s whole existence was about getting enough to survive, and then suddenly, survival meant more than just food. It meant not saying the wrong thing, not being seen with the wrong people, not looking too eager or too slow at meetings. I watched neighbors disappear from their doorways. I saw a teacher in our village forced to kneel in front of the school gate, his face swollen, his hands tied with rough rope. He was accused of “old thinking.” I was told to shout at him, and I did, because not shouting would have marked me out. There was nowhere to hide.

Even in the army, there was no escape. The barracks were filled with talk about class background and loyalty. You ate, drilled, and even slept under portraits of Mao, his gaze following you everywhere. The only relief was in the rhythm of work—scrubbing, hauling, running—because when your body was exhausted, your mind had less room for fear.

When I got to Peking University, I thought maybe things would be different. But even there, the old world was gone. The campus was full of banners and slogans. The lectures were half political meetings. The military structure followed me into the dormitory. You could feel the tension in the air, like the whole place might explode again at any moment.

You talk about not knowing what to ask. For me, the only question was always: how do I get through this without being crushed? When I was finally lifted up—given that badge, that student ID—it wasn’t separation from fear. It was being handed a shield, for the first time in my life. But I never forgot what it cost others. I saw who was missing in the lecture halls, who had been pushed out so I could sit there. That shield was heavy. I still feel its weight now.

Moderator: The dialogue accurately reflects the diversity of experiences during the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR’s and Researcher’s accounts of humiliation and lost professional order are consistent with the persecution of intellectuals and shifting power dynamics in work units. RedGuard’s admission of learned numbness and peer pressure aligns with research on group psychology and the dangers of ideological conformity. CRTeenFromBeijing’s sheltered perspective is plausible, as military compounds often provided relative protection, but even there, fear and secrecy were common. CRBeneficiary’s vivid depiction of rural hardship, political scrutiny, and the ambiguous relief of upward mobility through political channels is historically accurate—rural areas often experienced the harshest violence and social upheaval. All participants’ memories are in line with documented realities, including the emotional and moral complexities of the era.
